prompt: Two images in different repositories have the same digest. What can you conclude?
hint: A digest is a hash of the content.

choices.text: They were pushed by the same pipeline run
choices.why: Nothing in a digest records who pushed or when.

choices.text: They carry the same tag
choices.why: Tags are names kept beside the image; the same image can carry different ones in each repository.

choices.text: They are the same image
choices.why: Right. The same content gives the same digest, wherever it is stored.

choices.text: They were built from the same Dockerfile on different days
choices.why: Two builds of one Dockerfile usually differ in some layer, and then the digests differ.

prompt: A service's tasks all run `shop/web:latest`. Two of them restart after a new push; the others do not. What is running now?
hint: When does a task resolve the tag?

choices.text: Every task runs the new build, because the tag moved
choices.why: A running task keeps the image it pulled; only a restart asks the tag again.

choices.text: Two versions at once, under one name
choices.why: Right. The restarted tasks pulled the new image; the rest still run the old one.

choices.text: The old build everywhere, until the service is redeployed
choices.why: The two that restarted asked for latest and got whatever it pointed at then.

choices.text: Nothing, because ECR refuses to serve a tag that moved
choices.why: A mutable repository serves whatever the tag points at now, with no complaint.

prompt: Why could this lesson not run `docker push` against moto?
hint: Two protocols are involved in a push.

choices.text: Because Docker refuses to log in with the test key
choices.why: The login is not where it stops; moto has no registry to log in to.

choices.text: Because moto only accepts images under 50 MB
choices.why: No size limit is involved; no layer reaches moto at all.

choices.text: Because a push needs an AWS account to bill the storage
choices.why: moto bills nothing and needs no account; the missing piece is a protocol.

choices.text: moto answers PutImage but not the registry protocol
choices.why: Right. The layers travel over the registry protocol, which moto does not speak; PutImage is the last step only.

prompt: In an `IMMUTABLE` repository, `1.4.0` already points at an image. A pipeline pushes different content as `1.4.0`. What happens?

choices.text: The tag moves and the old image becomes untagged
choices.why: That is what a mutable repository does.

choices.text: ECR stores the new image as 1.4.0-2
choices.why: ECR never invents a tag; the push simply fails.

choices.text: Both images keep the tag 1.4.0, told apart by their digests
choices.why: A tag points at one image in a repository, never at two.

choices.text: The push is refused, and 1.4.0 keeps its image
choices.why: Right. ECR answers ImageTagAlreadyExistsException; the old image is untouched.

prompt: An immutable repository already holds an image tagged `1.4.1`. Can the pipeline add the tag `3f9c2a1b7e40` to that same image?
hint: Immutability is about moving a tag.

choices.text: No: an immutable image cannot gain tags after its first push
choices.why: Immutability protects tags from moving, and adding a new one moves nothing.

choices.text: Only by deleting 1.4.1 first
choices.why: Nothing has to be deleted; an image may carry several tags.

choices.text: Yes, as long as that tag is not taken
choices.why: Right. The lab did exactly that, and the image carries both.

choices.text: Yes, but the repository has to be switched to MUTABLE first
choices.why: No switch is needed; a free tag can be given in an immutable repository.

prompt: A team wants every release tag fixed, but developers' `dev-` builds overwritten freely, in one repository. Which setting does it?

choices.text: MUTABLE, and a lifecycle rule that keeps releases
choices.why: A lifecycle rule deletes images; it never stops a tag from moving.

choices.text: IMMUTABLE_WITH_EXCLUSION, filtered on dev-*
choices.why: Right. Tags matching the filter may move; every other tag stays fixed.

choices.text: IMMUTABLE_WITH_EXCLUSION, filtered on *
choices.why: A filter of * excludes every tag, which is a mutable repository with a longer name.

choices.text: IMMUTABLE, with developers deleting their old tags before each push
choices.why: It works by hand and fails the first busy day; the exclusion does it for them.

prompt: A mutable tag is a pointer; what identifies the image itself is its ___, a hash of its manifest.
hint: Six letters, starts with sha256: when written out.

prompt: What does enhanced scanning do that basic scanning does not?
hint: Think of a vulnerability published next week.

choices.text: It scans the image at every push, where basic scanning never does
choices.why: Basic scanning can scan on push too; scanOnPush is a setting of both.

choices.text: It blocks the push of an image with findings
choices.why: Neither blocks a push; a gate in the pipeline does that.

choices.text: It rescans when new vulnerabilities are published, and reads language packages
choices.why: Right. Inspector rescans continuously and covers Python, npm and other libraries.

choices.text: It is free
choices.why: Basic scanning is the free one; enhanced is billed by Inspector per image and rescan.

prompt: The lab's scan returned `CVE-9999-9999` in a package called `moto_fake`. What does that show about the scan-gate script?
hint: Separate the logic from its input.

choices.text: That the gate refuses a high finding, though this one is fake
choices.why: Right. The logic was exercised; the input was a placeholder.

choices.text: That the image has a high vulnerability to fix
choices.why: moto returns that finding for every image; it read nothing.

choices.text: Nothing, because the script should have ignored it
choices.why: The script cannot know a finding is fake; it counts severities as it should.

choices.text: That scanning works the same in moto as in ECR
choices.why: It shows the opposite: the API shape is the same and the finding is invented.

prompt: A gate refusing every finding of every severity has blocked deployments for a week, and the team is about to turn it off. What keeps protection without that?
hint: A line people can live with, plus fixes upstream.

choices.text: Run the gate only on Fridays
choices.why: A gate that runs on one day lets six days of images through unchecked.

choices.text: Refuse on critical and high, rebuild on fresh base images, allow dated exceptions
choices.why: Right. A narrower line stays on, rebuilds remove most findings, and exceptions expire.

choices.text: Switch from enhanced to basic scanning so fewer findings appear
choices.why: Seeing less is not the same as being safer.

choices.text: Keep the gate but let any developer bypass it with a commit message
choices.why: A bypass anybody can type becomes the normal path within a week.

prompt: With enhanced scanning at 0.11 USD per first scan and 0.01 USD per rescan, what does a month cost in which 300 new images are pushed and 2,000 rescans happen?
hint: Two lines of the price list, added.

prompt: Rule 1 expires untagged images after 7 days; rule 2 keeps the 30 newest images tagged `dev-`. An image is tagged `1.4.0`. Which rule can expire it?
hint: Which rule selects it at all?

choices.text: Rule 1, once it is seven days old
choices.why: Rule 1 selects untagged images only, and this one has a tag.

choices.text: Rule 2, when 30 newer dev builds arrive
choices.why: Rule 2 selects tags starting with dev-, and 1.4.0 does not.

choices.text: Neither: no rule selects it
choices.why: Right. An image no rule selects is never expired.

choices.text: Both, whichever has the lower priority
choices.why: Priority orders rules that select an image; here neither does.

prompt: Before new expiry rules go live on a repository production pulls from, what should be run first, and why?
hint: A rule written slightly wrong can delete what is running.

choices.text: start-lifecycle-policy-preview, to list what would expire
choices.why: Right. The preview evaluates the rules and deletes nothing.

choices.text: A scan of every image, so no vulnerable image is kept
choices.why: Scanning has nothing to say about which images the rules will delete.

choices.text: A restart of every task, so they all pull fresh images first
choices.why: Restarting is the moment a deleted image would bite, not a check.

choices.text: Nothing: ECR refuses to expire an image that is running
choices.why: ECR does not know what runs; a running task fails only when it restarts.

prompt: Put the steps of a push to a registry in the order they happen.
items: The client logs in to the registry
Each layer the registry lacks is uploaded as a blob
The manifest is uploaded under a tag
The registry points the tag at the manifest's digest
trap: Sending the manifest first is the slip: it names layers the registry would not have yet.

prompt: Match each ECR setting to what it protects against.

pairs.right: A release name moving to other code
An image nobody checked for known vulnerabilities
Thousands of old builds growing on the bill
Not knowing which code is running

prompt: Production runs `shop/api:3f9c2a1b7e40` from an immutable repository, and the release broke checkout. What does rolling back to the previous image require?
hint: A tag that cannot have moved.

choices.text: Rebuilding the previous commit and pushing it again
choices.why: A rebuild can differ from what ran; the previous image is still there, unchanged.

choices.text: Moving latest back to the old digest
choices.why: Nothing here deploys by latest, and in an immutable repository it would not move.

choices.text: A deployment naming the previous tag
choices.why: Right. The old tag still points at exactly the image that ran before.

choices.text: Asking ECR to restore the image from its version history
choices.why: ECR keeps no version history of a tag; immutability is what makes one unnecessary.
